Whistleblower Jodi O’Malley comes aboard the Lucky Charm III to share what her life’s been like since she heroically exposed how the federal government was handling (and allegedly hiding) adverse reactions to the COVID-19 vaccine.

In 2021, Jodi was a nurse at the Phoenix Indian Medical Center, a facility under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She tells James how the Holy Spirit prompted her to hit “record” while her concerned colleagues, including physicians, were discussing patients they believed were suffering adverse effects from the vaccine, reactions that weren't being formally reported. Thus, igniting Jodi’s ongoing advocacy in nursing.

Jodi also shares other challenging moments in her life that strengthened her faith and trust in God, leading her to the work and mission she’s tackling now.

Cisco UCS and UCS-Based Appliances UEFI Shell Secure Boot Bypass Vulnerability
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ucs-uefi-sb-bypass-eb6xC5GW?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20UCS%20and%20UCS-Based%20Appliances%20UEFI%20Shell%20Secure%20Boot%20Bypass%20Vulnerability%26vs_k=1

A vulnerability in the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Shell implementation of Cisco UCS Servers and UCS-based appliances could allow an authenticated attacker with valid credentials for a user account with the role of user or admin or an unauthenticated attacker with physical access to an affected device to bypass UEFI Secure Boot validation checks and execute unauthorized software.
This vulnerability is due to the availability of memory write commands in the UEFI Shell while UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by selecting the UEFI Shell boot option at boot time and using available shell commands to modify UEFI memory variables. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, overwrite UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, and execute unauthorized software on the affected device.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.
This advisory is available at the following link:

Musk officially confirmed: the first Optimus robots will go on sale in 2027.

And the bet on them is so massive that, to make room for these robots, the company has already discontinued its legendary Model S and Model X cars.

Tesla wants to create a truly universal assistant: clean the house, put things away, bring in groceries, load the washing machine, open the door, use regular tools, and learn new tasks simply by being told what to do.

In short, a new member of the family for every household. And on top of that, a universal worker in any factory.

The target price is around $20–30K, although Tesla has not announced the final price yet.

Right now, in Texas, they are designing a factory to produce 10 million robots a year. That’s 20 times more than the number of robots being made worldwide right now.

So Tesla is going almost all-in on this field.

Although the bet is worth it. If Optimus learns to work like a human, for the first time, the workforce could simply be produced on an assembly line. And here’s a solution to demographic problems around the world.

​Urgent news: GPT-6 Astra has just passed ALL 48 levels of the "I am not a robot" CAPTCHA.

OpenAI engineer Sharif Shamim watched as Astra navigated through all the existing CAPTCHA challenges, which range from simple image recognition to parking, chess, puzzles, and interactive UI challenges.

Astra completed all tasks designed to distinguish between humans and bots, utilizing its computer abilities to understand what is happening on the screen and directly perform actions.

If you have not yet realized what has happened, the world has become less secure from today onwards. Any user of GPT-6 Astra can now crack any existing CAPTCHA in the world. This means they can write any exploits to bypass CAPTCHA and launch attacks on any websites.

Credit must be given to security engineers; figuratively speaking, they are not sleeping and are continuously working to enhance security measures.

As traditional CAPTCHAs (ReCAPTCHA v2, hCaptcha) are increasingly being hacked by automation, the industry is shifting towards behavioral analysis (e.g., ReCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile).

These methods work seamlessly for users, analyzing mouse movements, browser history, IP address, and other parameters to differentiate between humans and bots without the need to click on images.

However, as you may have already understood, all these tactics will not stop GPT-6 Astra, as it is constantly active, decoding every trick faster than they can be devised.

The initial models of Chat GPT were ridiculed by cybersecurity experts, claiming things like: "Your AI won't even be able to pass a CAPTCHA, what kind of intelligence is that?" But with the emergence of GPT-6 Astra, cybersecurity professionals are no longer laughing.

Moreover, not only can the new AI models crack any CAPTCHA, but they now prevent the creation of anything new that could stay functional for even a couple of hours.

Now that Astra is available not only to cybersecurity companies and white hats but also to nefarious actors, including the Lazarus Group (a well-known state-sponsored hacking group operating for North Korea's intelligence services), the situation is concerning.

When Klaus Schwab predicted to us a "massive cyberattack" followed by a blackout, it was funny. Now, not so much.
